ThingDef.label: stale wet cloth
ThingDef.description: An absorbent cloth draped over the body. No one knows how long it has been used. It cools the wearer, and in this heat, staying alive matters more than health.

ThingDef.label: dry hardened mud coating
ThingDef.description: Although it feels terrible against the skin, it at least helps the wearer endure heat.

ThingDef.label: reed shade wrap
ThingDef.description: A loose wrap woven from dry reeds. It barely counts as clothing, but it keeps the sun off and lets hot air through.

ThingDef.label: soaked bark shade wrap
ThingDef.description: Bark strips soaked in water and tied across the body. The smell is awful, but the first hours of heat are easier.

ThingDef.label: mud and reed cooling mantle
ThingDef.description: A heavy mat of mud and reeds. It is ugly, damp, and surprisingly useful under a merciless sun.

ThingDef.label: thick cooling mud shell
ThingDef.description: Several layers of dried mud cover the body. It cracks with every movement, but it keeps unbearable heat away.

ThingDef.label: single hemp warming layer
ThingDef.description: A thin piece of rough hemp cloth. It is not much, but it is better than bare skin.

ThingDef.label: layered hemp warming clothes
ThingDef.description: The most primitive hemp cloth, woven layer upon layer. It is ugly, but warm enough.

ThingDef.label: straw and bark quilt
ThingDef.description: Dry straw and bark stitched between old cloth. It crackles when the wearer moves, yet holds a little precious warmth.

ThingDef.label: patched fur scrap cloak
ThingDef.description: Scraps of fur sewn into a short cloak. The seams are open and the smell is worse, but wind cannot pass through easily.

ThingDef.label: smoke stiffened blanket
ThingDef.description: A blanket hardened by smoke and grease. It is coarse and dirty, but it keeps the cold away.

ThingDef.label: thick hide and hemp wrap
ThingDef.description: Several layers of hide and hemp tied around the body. It restricts no vital movement and holds warmth better than it looks.
